prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle and the experimental discovery of correlated and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene, opening moiré flat-band quantum matter

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a rare case in which a quantitative theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model of 2011) was followed by an experimental discovery (correlated insulators and superconductivity, 2018) that confirmed it and then spawned a whole field. The control parameter is geometric, the twist angle, and strong correlations arise from kinetic-energy quenching. That is exactly the kind of many-body mechanism a statistical physicist finds compelling. The result has been reproduced by many groups and carried over to other moiré platforms, including transition-metal dichalcogenides and fractional Chern states, so the discovery is stable even though the field keeps moving. The theory-plus-experiment structure maps onto a three-person credit without leaving the credited set. A citation framed around flat-band correlated physics, and not around the pairing mechanism, avoids the open questions.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity. The decisive experiments are seven to eight years old, the superconducting pairing mechanism is still debated, and twist-angle disorder and strain complicate how much of the reported phenomenology is intrinsic. There is also an attribution problem that the supplied names do not resolve. Yuan Cao and the other MIT experimental co-authors, and the parallel experimental groups, are outside the credited set, so the experimental half rests on a group leader's name alone. If the committee judges that interpretation must settle before recognition, B004 is the safer choice. It has been confirmed for nearly two decades, is well past the point where such objections arise, and was ranked highly by almost everyone.

responses.point: The moiré field is young, the nature of the superconductivity and correlated phases is debated, and it is unclear which specific discovery is the prize-worthy core.
responses.response: I accept the maturity concern but think the core can be defined sharply. The prediction of flat bands at a magic angle and the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle are independently reproduced, and that is what the citation should cover. Whether the pairing is phonon-mediated or electronic is a question about a derived phase and not about the discovery. I would not wait for it to be settled. Your own ranking of B009 at third and your note on the credit boundary suggest we agree on the substance and differ on timing. My concern is that waiting for a mechanism may mean waiting indefinitely, as with other unconventional superconductors.

responses.point: B004 is first: Z2 topological insulators reshaped how band structures are computed and searched, with very high originality, long confirmation, and a defensible theory-plus-experiment trio.
responses.response: I agree that B004 is the more mature case, and I ranked it second myself, so we are not far apart. Your point that electronic-structure theory can predict a striking regime in advance applies equally to twisted bilayers, where the continuum model anticipated the magic angle, and that is why I put B009 first. Where I differ from you is the novelty. The Z2 classification extends the topological programme already recognised in 2016, while moiré flat bands introduce a different control principle, geometry, which is not a corollary of the earlier topological work. I would not call the overlap disqualifying, but it is a real reason to weigh B009 slightly higher if the committee wants a new direction.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are a clean, original and transformative advance in precision, very mature, and with redefinition of the second pending. Moiré physics is slightly early, and the hBN dependence is a compound-discovery worry.
responses.response: I respect the cleanliness of B006, and I ranked it eighth because I read it as precision refinement building on the 2005 and 2012 prizes, not as a new principle. That is a judgement and I accept that it is contestable. On your hBN point, I think that the dependence on encapsulation in device fabrication is a technical enabler of cleaner samples and does not change who predicted and who discovered the flat-band correlated states. The superconductivity and insulators were seen in the first devices. I would keep B017 out of the credit, and I see no reason to broaden the citation.

responses.point: B004 is a natural and timely follow-up to the 2016 prize, with a sharp, testable prediction and a large durable programme, though the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang leaves an unresolved attribution question.
responses.response: I agree that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap is real and I do not think it can be repaired within the supplied names. A quantum spin Hall prize that credits Molenkamp for the HgTe observation without the HgTe proposal is awkward, and Zhang's death limits what the committee can do. This is my main reason for not ranking B004 first. B009 has a cleaner two-sided structure, a prediction and a discovery, with the main gaps on the experimental junior side, which is a more conventional and familiar problem. I read your fairness remark as a mild point in favour of B009, though I am aware that is a debatable reading.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the unresolved superconducting mechanism and the youth of the field as a reason to wait; this is the decisive question between B009 and B004.
Priority of the twist-angle idea relative to earlier band-structure work is judged from my own recollection and is not verified from the supplied text.
Whether Yuan Cao and other experimental co-authors should be credited, which the supplied names do not allow.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission and the overlap with the 2016 prize are enough to make B004 a weaker choice than I currently judge.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. His documented co-authors and institutions do not include any credited name on the shortlist, and he is a statistical physicist of complex systems and not a moiré or topological-matter specialist.
